raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to extend the benefits of drug-eluting stents (DES) while avoiding permanent metallic caging. The intended sequence is transient radial support, antiproliferative drug delivery, endothelial healing, progressive resorption, and—ultimately—restoration of vasomotion and adaptive remodeling. Early human experience with the poly-L-lactic acid Igaki-Tamai scaffold showed feasibility and long-term disappearance of struts, but also substantial repeat revascularization, emphasizing the challenge of combining adequate early strength with safe late degradation [1]. The everolimus-eluting Absorb scaffold then became the dominant clinical platform: first-in-human ABSORB studies demonstrated low early event rates, late lumen preservation, vasomotion, and imaging evidence of scaffold integration/resorption [2–5]. Porcine histology helped interpret optical coherence tomography findings and confirmed that apparent OCT “struts” during follow-up could represent proteoglycan-rich footprints rather than intact polymer [6].

The clinical promise of Absorb was tested in randomized trials. ABSORB II initially showed broadly similar 1-year clinical outcomes versus cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents, but its 3-year coprimary vasomotion and lumen-loss endpoints were not met and device-related events accumulated [7,8]. ABSORB III established 1-year noninferiority for target-lesion failure in selected lesions, supporting regulatory approval, but 3-year follow-up showed excess target-vessel myocardial infarction and device thrombosis, particularly in small vessels [9,10]. ABSORB Japan and ABSORB China also met early angiographic or clinical noninferiority endpoints, illustrating that in simple lesions, with careful sizing, first-generation BVS could approximate contemporary DES at 1 year [11,12]. A patient-level pooled analysis reinforced similar 1-year composite outcomes while highlighting a numerically higher thrombosis signal [13].

Subsequent all-comer and higher-risk studies changed the field’s trajectory. AIDA, designed to reflect routine PCI, reported similar target-vessel failure but substantially more definite/probable device thrombosis with BVS [14]. ABSORB IV attempted to correct earlier limitations with stricter vessel sizing, mandated lesion preparation, high-pressure post-dilation, and blinded symptom assessment; 1-year results were noninferior, yet 5-year follow-up still showed a modest excess of target-lesion failure, concentrated before expected completion of resorption [15,16]. COMPARE-ABSORB in patients at high restenosis risk met noninferiority for target-lesion failure but had higher device thrombosis and target-vessel myocardial infarction, leading to premature discontinuation [17]. Across ABSORB studies, implantation technique emerged as a key modifier: avoidance of small vessels, aggressive predilation, accurate sizing, and high-pressure noncompliant post-dilation (“PSP”) were associated with better outcomes but did not fully eliminate early hazard [18].

Meta-analyses clarified the time-dependent risk-benefit profile. At 2 years, Absorb increased target-lesion failure and device thrombosis compared with metallic DES [19]. Longer pooled analyses suggested that excess risk was greatest during the bioresorption phase and attenuated thereafter, supporting the biological rationale but underscoring the clinical cost of thick struts, limited expansion latitude, and dismantling-related thrombosis [20]. These findings led to withdrawal or marked restriction of first-generation PLLA BVS use and shifted emphasis toward improved scaffold design and niche indications.

Metallic bioresorbable scaffolds, particularly magnesium platforms, represent a second major strategy. The early PROGRESS-AMS magnesium stent proved feasibility but suffered rapid loss of radial support and restenosis [21]. Drug-eluting absorbable metal scaffolds improved performance: BIOSOLVE-I provided multimodality evidence of controlled degradation, and BIOSOLVE-II showed encouraging 6-month outcomes with the sirolimus-eluting DREAMS 2G/Magmaris scaffold [22,23]. Real-world BIOSOLVE-IV and extended BIOSOLVE-II follow-up suggested low scaffold thrombosis and acceptable target-lesion failure, although these were largely single-arm or registry data rather than definitive DES comparisons [24,25].

BVS may be biologically attractive in acute coronary syndromes, where younger patients and soft plaques are common, but trial data remain mixed. ISAR-Absorb MI found no advantage over everolimus-eluting stents in myocardial infarction, while TROFI II follow-up suggested preserved safety and potential vasomotor recovery signals in STEMI [26,27]. Smaller randomized and imaging studies such as EVERBIO-2 provide reassurance regarding late resorption but are underpowered for clinical events [28]. Newer platforms, including thinner-strut PLLA scaffolds such as NeoVas and broader pooled ABSORB-program analyses, indicate that design evolution and meticulous technique can improve—but have not yet proven superiority over excellent contemporary DES [29,30].

Thus, current evidence supports BVS as an instructive but not routine PCI technology. First-generation Absorb validated the concept of vascular restoration, but its excess thrombosis and myocardial infarction during resorption outweighed theoretical late benefits. Future success will require thinner struts, stronger radial support with predictable degradation, wider expansion tolerance, radiopacity, deliverability, imaging-guided implantation, and randomized evidence against modern ultrathin DES in carefully selected lesions.
